title: Whisky Miniatures and Sample Sets | Craft Beer School
desc: Whisky miniatures and sample sets: Indian bottle sizes, how many pours a mini gives, how small bottles keep and the legal line on decanting.
teaser: A 50 ml miniature is two proper tasting pours. That makes it the cheapest whisky lesson you can buy.
standfirst: Small bottles let you taste a whisky before committing to a full bottle. Sample sets go further and turn five bottles into a tasting flight. Here is how to use them well and what to watch for.
sections: Small bottles let you taste before you commit

A full bottle of a new whisky is a big commitment, especially at Indian prices. A small bottle lets you try it first. The common international miniature is 50 ml. Indian shelves use their own sizes: 90 ml and 180 ml (the quarter), 375 ml (the half) and 750 ml (the full bottle).

A 50 ml miniature is two 25 ml tasting pours, or one 30 ml pour with a little left to revisit. That is enough to know whether you like a whisky. A 180 ml quarter is enough for a proper evening's study.
Sample sets turn a shelf into a flight

Sample sets bundle three to six small bottles, often 20 to 50 ml each, around a theme: regions, cask types, ages or a distillery's core range. They are a ready-made tasting flight.

Good sets are designed to show contrast, such as a bourbon cask beside a sherry cask of the same spirit. That is far more useful than five random whiskies. Read the list before you buy and check that the set teaches something.

Whisky does not age in the bottle. Once sealed, it stays largely the same for years. Once opened, air starts to change it slowly. A small bottle, half empty, has a lot of air for very little whisky, so it changes faster.

Store miniatures upright, away from heat and sunlight. Cork stoppers can dry out in Indian heat; screw caps seal better for long storage. Once opened, finish a miniature within weeks rather than months. Our guide to storing an opened bottle covers the detail.
Why miniatures cost more per millilitre

A miniature almost always costs more per millilitre than the full bottle. The glass, cap, label, filling and excise paperwork cost nearly as much for a small bottle as for a large one, so those costs are spread over far less whisky.

Do the sum before you buy. Divide the price by the volume and multiply by 100 to get a price per 100 ml, then compare with the full bottle. A miniature at twice the per-millilitre price can still be a bargain if it stops you buying a 750 ml bottle you would not enjoy. That is the real value of a sample: it is insurance against an expensive mistake.

Decanting from a large bottle into small glass sample bottles is a common trick. It slows oxidation in a bottle you are drinking slowly, because the whisky in each small bottle has little air above it. It also lets you share whisky with friends and compare with them later.

Use clean glass bottles with good caps. Label each one with the name, strength and the date you filled it. Avoid plastic for anything you plan to keep, since it can pass on flavours.

Sharing a little whisky with friends at home is one thing. Selling decanted samples is selling liquor, which in India needs a licence. Excise rules vary by state and change, so do not sell or trade samples without checking.

Carrying small bottles between states is covered by the same limits as full bottles. Small size is not an exemption.
How to taste a set properly

Use the same glass for each sample, ideally a tulip-shaped nosing glass. Pour 15 to 20 ml. Taste in a planned order: lighter and lower strength first, peated and cask strength last, because smoke and high alcohol linger.

Taste one or two samples per evening rather than the whole set at once. Keep water alongside and add a few drops to each sample after your first sip. Our guide to whisky tasting for beginners walks through the method.

A sample only earns its price if you remember what it taught you. Write a few lines on each: nose, palate, finish, what water changed and whether you would buy the full bottle. A sample you tasted and forgot was just a small drink.

Over a few months, those notes become a personal map of what you like. That is worth more than any rating in a magazine, because it is built on your own palate.

Pick three small bottles that differ in one clear way, such as an unpeated, a lightly peated and a heavily peated whisky. Taste them on the same evening, 15 ml each, in that order.

Write down where the smoke first appeared for you and which you would buy. That one flight will tell you more about your taste than a shelf of full bottles.
faqs: How many pours are in a whisky miniature?
A 50 ml miniature gives two 25 ml tasting pours, or one 30 ml pour with a little left to revisit.
How long does a miniature keep once opened?
Weeks rather than months. A part-empty small bottle has a lot of air for little whisky, so it changes faster.
Can I sell whisky samples I decant myself?
Selling liquor in India needs a licence. Rules vary by state. Do not sell or trade samples without checking.
